title: Mechanical Roots
content: Before the electric era, the basic ideas of a "computer" were born as complex mechanical machines.

title: Charles Babbage & The Analytical Engine
content: Babbage designed a mechanical machine containing all the elements of a modern computer: a processing unit (Mill), memory (Store), and I/O. This is the ancestor of the general-purpose computer.

title: Ada Lovelace (The First Programmer)
content: Lovelace wrote the first algorithm intended to be executed by a machine (calculating Bernoulli numbers), realizing the machine could process general symbols and not just numbers.

title: Theory & The Wartime Need
content: World War II created a massive drive for fast calculation capabilities for ballistics and cryptography.

title: Alan Turing & The Universal Machine
content: Turing laid the theoretical foundations for computer science with the "Turing Machine" – a mathematical model of a machine capable of performing any algorithmic calculation given the correct instructions.

title: Cracking the Enigma (Bletchley Park)
content: Turing and his team developed the Bombe to decipher the German 'Enigma' encryption machine. Concurrently, the Colossus, the first programmable electronic computer, was developed for intelligence purposes.

title: The Birth of the Modern Electronic Computer
content: The transition from dedicated machines to programmable computers based on vacuum tubes.

title: The ENIAC: The First Electronic Computer
content: The first general-purpose electronic computer. It weighed 30 tons, contained 18,000 vacuum tubes, and was 1,000 times faster than mechanical machines. Programming it required manual physical wiring of cables.

title: Von Neumann Architecture
content: Defining the structure where software and data are stored in the same memory (Stored-program). A revolution that allowed immediate software changes without hardware modification, forming the basis for modern RAM and CPUs.

title: The Basic Instruction Cycle (No Interrupts)
content: The first practical implementation of the Von Neumann model (such as in the Manchester Baby). The processor executes a simple Fetch-Decode-Execute cycle serially, without an interrupt mechanism.

title: The Era of the Transistor and Chips
content: Computers became smaller, more efficient, and cheaper thanks to the invention of the transistor and the integrated circuit.

title: Invention of the Transistor
content: Replacing vacuum tubes with a small, reliable, and cooler component. The turning point in electronics that enabled computer miniaturization.

title: The First Microprocessor (Intel 4004)
content: Compressing the entire processing unit onto a single tiny silicon chip. This invention paved the way for personal computers.

title: Development of x86 Architecture
content: Launch of the Intel 8086 processor. Its instruction set became the industrial standard for personal computers and servers, and it dominates the computing market to this day.

title: The Transition to 64-bit (x86-64)
content: An AMD development that enabled wide data processing and the use of RAM larger than 4GB, while maintaining backward compatibility with older software.

title: The Era of Multi-Core and AI
content: Transitioning to processors with multiple cores (Multi-Core) to improve performance without overheating, and using graphics accelerators (GPUs) for massive artificial intelligence calculations.
